subject: Sizing: burst vs sustained capacity decomposition for LodeStar pilot
messages:
From: Evan Cho <ops@lodestar.ai>
To: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>
Cc: Priya Shah <pri@lodestar.ai>
Date: Fri, 14 Jun 2024 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Pilot sizing question — burst vs sustained

Hi Marcus,

We're lining up a 6-week pilot with Redwood and trying to understand how to size dedicated capacity for our conversational inference workload. High level: we have a production-ish traffic pattern that is relatively steady but with short sharp marketing-driven bursts (minutes-long) during campaigns. We need to decide how much reserved GPU capacity to request vs relying on burst/buffer.

Quick sketch of what we can share now:
- Typical daily active users: ~18k, MAU growth expected 15% month-over-month for the pilot
- Baseline traffic window: 09:00–21:00 PT; sustained traffic averages ~75 requests/sec across services during that window
- Campaign bursts: historically spike up to ~420 requests/sec for ~6–18 minutes (one or two times per day)
- Prompts: average prompt length ~100 tokens, average generated response ~380 tokens (some multimodal pieces, but mostly text)
- Preferred model family: open-chat-70B quantized (internal ops preference)
- Latency target: p99 end-to-end < 450ms (streaming acceptable)

Can Redwood put together a recommended reserved footprint (GPU SKU mix + redundancy) plus an approach for handling the daily burst windows (reserved + burst credit vs autoscaling)? Also curious how prefix caching/KV cache might change the numbers since many of the campaigns reuse similar context.

I can share sample telemetry if you want (token histograms / session traces).

Thanks — Evan
Evan Cho
Head of SRE, LodeStar AI
ops@lodestar.ai

Evan — thanks for the context. This is exactly the kind of info we need. I've attached a brief worksheet that will let us decompose burst vs sustained capacity and show the math that drives SKU recommendations (lodestar_capacity_qna.xlsx). Can you fill the short fields below and return the sheet? If you can paste answers inline, that's fine too.

Short questionnaire (helps us to model):
1) Exact peak burst cadence: how often per day/week do you hit the 6–18 minute spikes?
2) Burst request pattern: is it uniform within the burst window or more choppy (very spiky sub-minute peaks)?
3) Session/connection behavior: are requests independent (stateless) or conversational sessions with KV cache reuse across messages? Typical session length and avg messages/session?
4) Cache expectations: estimated prefix/KV cache hit rate (0–100%) and percent of requests that benefit from cached KV (if known)
5) Model config: precise model name & quantization (e.g., open-chat-70B-qat/8bit) and whether you'd accept a slightly lower-capacity quantized variant for burst handling
6) Target operational redundancy: N+1 across racks, or can bursts be handled with fewer redundancy constraints?
7) Tolerance for graceful degradation: acceptable fallback model with higher latency but lower cost?

If you prefer, we can do a 30-minute call Monday to step through the worksheet.

Attachment: lodestar_capacity_qna.xlsx (spreadsheet)

Cheers,

From: Evan Cho <ops@lodestar.ai>

Date: Sun, 16 Jun 2024 10:23:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Pilot sizing question — burst vs sustained

Marcus — here are the answers; pasted below so you have them in-thread. I also uploaded a short token-histogram export to the Google Sheet link.

1) Peak burst cadence: Campaign-driven spikes happen 1–3 times per day on average during marketing windows (higher on launch days). Historically ~60% of days have at least one short spike; busiest days 3 spikes.
2) Burst shape: bursts are front-loaded (first 90–120 seconds very spiky) then decay — so sub-minute micro-peaks are common within the 6–18 minute window.
3) Session behavior: conversational sessions — avg messages/session = 3.4, median session length ~45s, 95th percentile session length ~220s. Requests benefit from KV reuse across the session.
4) Cache expectations: estimated KV/prefix cache hit rate ~22% for the conversational flows that reuse context; other stateless endpoints have negligible cache benefit.
5) Model: open-chat-70B-8q (we're testing an 8-bit quantized variant). We could consider a slightly smaller 34B quantized variant for burst overflow if it helps economics and keeps quality acceptable.
6) Redundancy: we'd like N+1 across failure domains but can tolerate temporarily falling back to lower SLA for brief bursts if we have a documented plan.
7) Graceful degradation: acceptable fallback is a 34B quantized model serving as overflow with increased latency up to 800ms p99 during burst fallback.

Hope that helps — happy to hop on a call.

Evan

Subject: Internal: LodeStar sizing — initial calc & recommendation draft

Laura / Tessa,

Looping you in with the answers from LodeStar so we can turn this into a concrete dedicated-reserved recommendation. High level math below (quick pass):
- Sustained footprint: 75 req/s sustained window * avg token per request (prompt+response = 480 tokens) = 36k tokens/sec sustained.
- Burst footprint: peak 420 req/s * same token mix = 201.6k tokens/sec during peak. Bursts are short (6–18 min) but include micro-peaks.
- Session accounting: with KV hit rate ~22%, effective tokens/sec drops approx 22% for conversational endpoints (apply to ~60% of requests), netting ~31k tokens/sec sustained (post-cache).

Sizing inference throughput to GPUs (very rough):
- Measured on our 70B-quantized profile: a single optimized 80GB GPU (quant queues + continuous batching) can sustain ~28–36k tokens/sec for steady small-latency loads with 8 concurrent streams, but degrades on large burst concurrency without aggressive oversubscription.

Recommendation (initial):
- Reserve a baseline pool of 3 x 80GB GPUs (handles sustained + small headroom) — this maps to ~90–100k tokens/sec effective when accounting for batching and cache. The math assumes sophisticated batching and max continuous KV reuse.
- Reserve a burst pool of 6 x 80GB GPUs as cold standby reserved capacity that we enable via autoscaler for campaign windows (gives headroom up to ~360–420k tokens/sec depending on batching). We suggest enabling elastic routing: traffic pins to reserved baseline unless burst policy triggers ephemeral capacity (can be reserved or on-host burst credits).
- Canary plan: route 30% of traffic to 34B-quant overflow during initial campaign to vet quality and reduce cost; automated failback if quality regressions detected by prompt tests.

Notes & questions for Evan to confirm:
- Are you able to accept a 30% canary to the smaller variant?
- Any hard constraint on rack-level redundancy that would force more distributed reserved capacity?

I've attached a calculation workbook with per-GPU tokens/sec assumptions and a cost delta summary (marcus_lodestar_sizing_calc.xlsx). If this looks reasonable I'll produce a short PDF recommendation and proposed deployment plan for signatures.

Marcus
Marcus Lin | Sales Engineer | Redwood Inference
marcus@redwood.com

Attachment: marcus_lodestar_sizing_calc.xlsx

From: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>
To: Evan Cho <ops@lodestar.ai>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura@redwood.com>, Tessa Morgan <tessa@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 18 Jun 2024 16:45:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Pilot sizing question — burst vs sustained (recommendation & next steps)

Evan — thanks for the quick answers and the sheet. Based on the inputs we ran the above baseline + burst decomposition and propose the following pilot footprint and operational plan:

1) Reserved baseline: 3 x 80GB GPUs (quantized 70B profile). Covers sustained window with N+1 redundancy across two racks. Estimated effective sustained throughput (post-caching & batching) ~95k tokens/sec.
2) Burst handling: 6 x 80GB GPUs reserved as a burst pool that we enable via autoscaler rules during campaign windows. Policy: scale to full burst pool when 90% of baseline token throughput sustained for 60s OR when request concurrency > 300 for 60s. The reserved burst pool gives headroom for the 6–18 minute windows and micro-peaks.
3) Overflow canary: route 30% of requests to a 34B-quantized variant during first two campaign days; automatic rollback on quality regression thresholds (we'll instrument with a small prompt test set).
4) KV caching: with the expected ~22% hit rate we factored in a 12–18% effective reduction in token load for conversational endpoints; we will enable prefix cache and hot-KV eviction tuned for ~5–10 minute session reuse.

Costs & next steps:
- We've attached a one-page recommended deployment plan and an estimated monthly cost delta (recommended_deployment_plan.pdf). If you want to reduce committed spend, alternatives: shrink burst pool to 4 GPUs and rely on short-lived on-demand capacity for rare spikes, or increase canary to 50% across bursts to move load to smaller instances faster.

Can you confirm the redundancy constraint and whether a 30% canary is acceptable for the first campaign? If yes, we'll schedule a handoff to engineering and prepare the Dedicated order sheet.

Cheers,
Marcus Lin
Sales Engineer | Redwood Inference
marcus@redwood.com
